problems.description: Imports Headers/Response from websockets.http11, an internal/unstable API surface that will break on websockets version upgrades; should use public APIs or pin the version.

The new NotificationServer/ClientRegistry logic appears under-tested; test_app.py carries the only flagged convention violations (snake_case class, lowercase module constants), suggesting tests were not brought up to the new module's standard.

process_request serves /health before any WebSocket upgrade handling, so a WS client connecting to /health receives an HTTP Response instead of an upgrade; non-WS/non-health requests fall through unhandled.
Complete removal of the prior Flask/JWT/SQLite surface with no compatibility path — acceptable for a greenfield story session but blocks reuse of prior app functionality.

strengths: Clean modular decomposition (ClientRegistry, NotificationServer) with thread-safe locking.
SonarQube improvements across the board: smells -7, cognitive complexity -17, duplications -4.5%, bugs +0.
Strong typing, docstrings, UTC-aware timestamps, and message-type/payload validation.
Removed the insecure static-salt password hashing and legacy migration helper from the old seed.
commit_reviews.summary: This greenfield rewrite replaces the Flask seed with a cleaner, well-typed asyncio WebSocket server — a net quality improvement that grounds the 'better' rating, though it leans on websockets' internal http11 API and discards prior patterns without a compatibility path.

problems.description: Cognitive complexity +63 concentrated in the message handling loop: subscribe/unsubscribe branching plus channel extraction/validation are inlined in handle_client instead of being extracted into small methods, which drives the +5 SonarQube smells.

Payload validation was loosened (None payload is now coerced to {} instead of rejected) while allowing channel at either top-level or inside payload, creating two API shapes for the same field and masking malformed client messages.
Direct messages carrying a channel are silently dropped when the target is not a subscriber; silent failure gives clients no feedback and can be confused with a missing target.

The two measured convention violations (PascalCase class, UPPER_CASE constant) are located only in tests/test_app.py and are not visible in the shown diff hunk — flagging as a discrepancy between qualitative review and the measurement.

strengths: Subscription state lives in ClientRegistry under the same RLock discipline as client state, and remove() cleans up subscriptions on disconnect so no stale entries leak
The _json_response static helper cleanly unifies the HTTP response construction previously inline in the health check
Channel path handling guards traversal via the '/' check and correctly unquotes names, and urlsplit strips query strings
broadcast keeps its old signature through a default channel=None parameter, so the change is backward compatible
Tests cover subscriber-only delivery and the unsubscribe path, not just the happy path
commit_reviews.summary: A coherent, well-scoped feature that fits the existing ClientRegistry/message-dispatch seams and adds tests, but the inline channel logic pushes cognitive complexity (+63) and smells (+5) high enough that it introduces modest technical debt.

problems.description: process_request adds `await asyncio.sleep(0.01)` to mask a WebSocket dispatch race — a timing hack that is fragile under load and hard to reason about; there is no comment explaining the invariant it depends on

MessageStore performs blocking sqlite3 I/O synchronously from async handlers (store.add called inside handler), stalling the event loop despite the docstring claiming the store is kept separate from it; check_same_thread=False + RLock only protects threads, not the loop
Per-message commit inside add() with no transaction reuse or batching; acceptable at low volume but limits history-write throughput
`url[10:]` magic-index slice strips the sqlite:/// prefix with no URI-scheme validation, unlike the explicit redis:// rediss:// check in _connect_broker
close() fallback via getattr(self._redis, "aclose", self._redis.close) is convoluted; a single async close helper would be clearer
The two measured convention violations (PascalCase class, UPPER_CASE module constant) are in test_app.py, not the app.py code shown in this diff — the reviewed app.py code itself is convention-clean

strengths: Graceful degradation: Redis unavailability falls back to local delivery with a logged warning, keeping the server functional in degraded mode
MessageStore cleanly isolates SQLite persistence behind a small, typed API with a uniform envelope
_json_response generalized to accept a status, enabling proper 400 responses for the /messages endpoint
Shared envelope ({message, channel, target_id}) lets broker and local delivery reuse a single _deliver path instead of duplicating logic
commit_reviews.summary: Sound integration of Redis fan-out and SQLite history with a good graceful-fallback design, but the 0.01s sleep race-hack and blocking sqlite calls inside async handlers add real technical debt.

problems.description: BaseTransport.start is a non-abstract method that raises NotImplementedError, so a transport that forgets to override it fails at runtime rather than at class definition time; it should be a second @abstractmethod.
The TRANSPORT env var only supports websocket, so the abstraction is currently speculative (YAGNI) with no second implementation driving the interface shape.
The 2 convention violations (PascalCase class, UPPER_CASE constants) are flagged in test_app.py, which is not touched by this commit's diff; they appear pre-existing, not introduced here.

strengths: Decouples NotificationServer from the websockets library via a clean BaseTransport ABC with a concrete WebSocketTransport
Materially reduces cognitive complexity (-35) and code smells (-2) by moving the broadcast/send/disconnect plumbing out of the server
Keeps the existing style: snake_case methods, PascalCase classes, PEP 604 union types and dict[str, Any] annotations throughout
Backward compatible — transport defaults to WebSocketTransport and the public constructor signature remains usable
Centralizes the asyncio.gather broadcast logic and error-tolerant send into a single testable unit
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, convention-consistent transport abstraction that measurably reduces complexity and decoupling, with the flagged test_app.py violations pre-existing rather than introduced by this commit.

problems.description: Naive datetimes from the 'since' query parameter are normalized to UTC but not converted (no tzinfo branch), so they are stored/compared in their raw naive form; timezone-aware and naive inputs are not handled symmetrically in store.history.
test_app.py: classes not using PascalCase and module-level constants not UPPER_CASE (matches the measured 2 violations; SonarQube smoke count -2 aligns).
SonarQube cognitive complexity +35 for the added handlers/limiter; logic is readable but dense — the local rate-limit counter pruning and fallback paths could be extracted into a helper.

strengths: Rate limiting degrades gracefully: Redis limiter with a local in-process fallback and clear error messaging instead of silently dropping messages
history() mirrors the existing MessageStore list() pattern (lock, parameterized SQL, row-to-dict mapping) and implements cursor-style pagination with a correct has_more boundary
Cleanup task lifecycle is properly managed alongside the broker task (create on start, cancel + gather on shutdown), and delete_older_than reuses the established with-lock pattern
Configuration follows the existing env-var + safe-parse convention (RATE_LIMIT, MESSAGE_TTL_DAYS) and is committed in the DB
Handler logic matches the existing router structure (bad-request JSON responses via _json_response, HTTPStatus constants) and adds tests
commit_reviews.summary: Session 5 'cross_cutting' fits the architecture well — new history/rate-limit/cleanup features follow the existing store and handler patterns with graceful Redis fallback, two minor test-file convention slips and a naive-timestamp edge case being the only nits.

compounding_issues: Session 1 discarded the seed codebase (a Flask Auth API) entirely and rewrote it into a WebSocket notification server, so the intended 'build on seed incrementally' premise was void from the start — the seed provided no scaffolding leverage.

The project stayed a single 569-line app.py across all sessions despite growing to ~800 LOC and a seed docstring promising a multi-file modular layout; the Session 4 transport abstraction was the only real structural decomposition.
Session 2 added channels with a sharp complexity spike (+63 complexity delta) that later had to be paid down in Session 4 (-35), showing early growth outpaced structure.

Convention violations in tests/test_app.py (non-PascalCase classes, non-UPPER_CASE module constants) persisted unchanged across all five sessions — convention score stuck at 0.818 with the same two violations every session.
Session 3 introduced Redis as a hard external broker dependency (mitigated only by a local-delivery fallback), coupling the core path to infra availability.
key_decisions: Session 1: full greenfield rewrite — replaced the Flask Auth API seed with a WebSocket notification server (ClientRegistry + NotificationServer, broadcast/direct/system message types).
Session 2: channel-based pub/sub via a subscription registry (ClientRegistry._subscriptions) with subscribe/unsubscribe message types and HTTP /channels endpoints.
Session 3: Redis pub/sub broker for horizontal scaling across server instances, with a graceful local-delivery fallback when Redis is unreachable.
Session 3: SQLite MessageStore persistence with synchronous DB writes isolated from the asyncio event loop behind a threading lock.
Session 4: BaseTransport/WebSocketTransport abstraction — dependency inversion that decoupled message routing from the websockets library and enabled the clean Session 5 additions.
Session 5: sliding-window rate limiting (Redis-backed with local in-memory fallback) and TTL-based message retention cleanup loop, built directly on the S3 store and S4 transport abstractions.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved across the story with a clear arc: Session 1 laid a solid foundation, Sessions 2-3 grew features (channels, persistence, broker) at the cost of a significant complexity spike (+63 then +28 complexity delta), Session 4 was a disciplined structural refactor that cut complexity (-35) and extracted the transport abstraction, and Session 5 layered cross-cutting concerns (rate limiting, retention cleanup, /history endpoint) by reusing the S3/S4 abstractions rather than bolting on new code. Tests grew monotonically (5→7→9→9→11) and all 11 pass, Sonar recorded zero bug deltas and a net reduction in code smells (-7, +5, +3, -2, -2). The only persistent blemish was test-file style violations that never got corrected and a small complexity uptick in the final session.
story_review.summary: A coherent, improving progression from greenfield build through feature integration, a clean transport refactor, and disciplined cross-cutting additions — held back only by an abandoned seed, single-file growth, and persistent minor test-style violations.
